questions.question: State the ACID properties of a database transaction and explain the role of the write-ahead log (WAL).
questions.justification: Directs the student to state the ACID properties and explain the specific logging mechanism of WAL.
questions.model_answer: ACID properties: Atomicity ensures all operations in a transaction complete successfully or none at all; Consistency ensures the database transitions from one valid state to another satisfying all integrity constraints; Isolation ensures concurrent transactions execute without interfering with each other; Durability ensures once a transaction commits, its changes survive system crashes. Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) requires that any change to database data must be recorded in the log on stable storage before the actual database page is modified on disk. This ensures atomicity and durability by enabling REDO during recovery after a crash and UNDO for aborted transactions.

rubric.criterion: Definition and explanation of Atomicity and Consistency
Definition and explanation of Isolation and Durability
Explanation of Write-Ahead Log (WAL) mechanics and rule enforcement
Explanation of WAL role in crash recovery (REDO/UNDO)

own_words_criteria: All-or-nothing execution model for transactions
Logging modifications to non-volatile storage prior to disk page updates
Guaranteeing crash persistence and rollback capability

questions.question: Differentiate between B-Tree and B+ Tree index structures in terms of range query performance.
questions.justification: Requires contrasting B-Tree and B+ Tree structures specifically focusing on range query execution.
questions.model_answer: In a B-Tree, both keys and associated data pointers/records are stored in internal nodes as well as leaf nodes. In a B+ Tree, all data pointers and records reside exclusively in the leaf nodes, while internal nodes store only routing keys and child pointers. For range queries, B+ Tree significantly outperforms B-Tree because all leaf nodes in a B+ Tree are linked together sequentially as a doubly linked list. This allows the database engine to locate the starting point of the range via tree traversal and then perform a fast sequential scan across leaf nodes without having to traverse back up and down the internal nodes of the tree.

rubric.criterion: Structural difference regarding data storage in internal vs. leaf nodes
Explanation of sequential leaf node linkage in B+ Trees
Comparison of I/O efficiency during range query execution

own_words_criteria: Storing data payloads solely in leaf nodes for B+ Trees
Using sequential leaf pointers for traversal
Avoiding redundant internal node lookups during interval scans

questions.question: Define Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF) and distinguish it from Third Normal Form (3NF).
questions.justification: Requires defining BCNF and distinguishing its strict structural requirements from 3NF.
questions.model_answer: Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF) is a stricter version of Third Normal Form (3NF). A relation schema R is in BCNF if for every non-trivial functional dependency X -> Y, X must be a superkey of R. In contrast, 3NF permits a functional dependency X -> Y where X is not a superkey, provided that Y is a prime attribute (part of any candidate key). Therefore, 3NF allows anomalies when a non-prime attribute determines another non-prime attribute, or when a prime attribute determines a superkey, whereas BCNF eliminates all redundancy due to functional dependencies by insisting that every determinant is a superkey.

rubric.criterion: Precise definition of BCNF using superkeys
Definition of 3NF conditions including prime attribute allowance
Clear distinction highlighting non-prime attribute determinants permitted in 3NF but disallowed in BCNF

own_words_criteria: Every determinant must be a superkey for BCNF
Permitting non-superkey determinants if the right-hand side is a prime attribute in 3NF
Elimination of overlap and dependency anomalies

questions.question: Explain the phantom read anomaly and describe how Serializable isolation level prevents it.
questions.justification: Asks to explain the phantom read concurrency phenomenon and describe the mechanism of the Serializable isolation level.
questions.model_answer: A phantom read anomaly occurs when a transaction executes a query satisfying a certain search condition, and a second concurrent transaction inserts new rows that match the search condition and commits. When the first transaction re-executes the query, it sees a different set of rows (the 'phantoms'), violating repeatability. The Serializable isolation level prevents this by ensuring complete isolation, typically implemented using predicate locking, index-range locks, or SSI (Serializable Snapshot Isolation). Index-range locks lock the index range associated with the query condition, blocking any concurrent insertions into that specific search space until the reading transaction completes.

rubric.criterion: Definition and scenario of phantom read anomaly involving row insertions
Description of Serializable isolation level guarantees
Explanation of locking mechanisms (such as index-range locks or predicate locks) used to prevent phantoms

own_words_criteria: New rows appearing in a repeated query range
Locking search predicates and index intervals
Ensuring complete serial equivalence of concurrent transactions

questions.question: Illustrate conflict serializability of a schedule using a precedence (serialization) graph.
questions.justification: Requires constructing and illustrating conflict serializability using a precedence graph for a schedule.
questions.model_answer: A precedence graph for a schedule S contains vertices representing the transactions participating in S. Directed edges T_i -> T_j are added if transaction T_i executes a write/read operation on an item X before transaction T_j executes a read/write operation on the same item X, and there is a conflict. Specifically, edges are drawn if: (1) T_j reads X after T_i writes X, (2) T_j writes X after T_i reads X, or (3) T_j writes X after T_i writes X. If the constructed precedence graph contains no directed cycles, the schedule is conflict serializable, and a topological sort of the graph yields a valid equivalent serial execution order.

rubric.criterion: Definition of nodes and edge creation rules for conflicting operations
Explanation of the three conflict scenarios (W-R, R-W, W-W)
Condition for conflict serializability (acyclicity and topological sort)

own_words_criteria: Nodes as transactions and edges representing operation conflicts
Checking for cycles in the directed graph
Topological sorting to derive serial execution order

questions.question: Given a relational schema R(A, B, C, D, E) with Functional Dependencies F = { A->BC, CD->E, B->D, E->A }. Determine the candidate keys of R, decompose R into BCNF, and analyze if the decomposition is lossless and dependency-preserving.
questions.justification: Requires comprehensive evaluation involving candidate key derivation, BCNF decomposition steps, and testing for lossless join and dependency preservation.
questions.model_answer:
Step 1: Find Attribute Closure and Candidate Keys.
Attributes present: {A, B, C, D, E}. Let's test closures:
A^+ = {A, B, C, D, E} (since A->BC, B->D, CD->E). Thus, A is a candidate key.
Let's check other attributes:
B^+ = {B, D}
C^+ = {C}
D^+ = {D}
E^+ = {E, A, B, C, D} (since E->A, A->BC, B->D). Thus, E is also a candidate key.
Candidate Keys are {A} and {E}.

Step 2: BCNF Decomposition.
Relation R(A, B, C, D, E) has FD B -> D which violates BCNF because B is not a superkey.
Decompose R into R1(B, D) and R2(A, B, C, E).
- R1(B, D): FD is B -> D. B is superkey of R1. R1 is in BCNF.
- R2(A, B, C, E): FDs restricted to R2: A -> BC, E -> A, B -> C (derived). Candidate keys of R2 are A and E.
Check BCNF for R2:
- A -> BC: A is a superkey of R2. Satisfies BCNF.
- E -> A: E is not a superkey of R2. Violates BCNF!
Decompose R2 into R3(E, A) and R4(A, B, C).
- R3(E, A): FD is E -> A. E is superkey of R3. In BCNF.
- R4(A, B, C): FD is A -> BC. A is superkey of R4. In BCNF.
Final BCNF Decomposition: {R1(B, D), R3(E, A), R4(A, B, C)}.

Step 3: Lossless Join Property Check.
Join R1 and R4 on common attributes? R1(B, D) and R4(A, B, C) intersect on B. Is B -> B,D or B -> A,C? No. Let's check intermediate join: R3(E, A) joined with R4(A, B, C) on A gives R5(A, B, C, E) with common attribute A and A -> B,C. Since A is a superkey of R4, this join is lossless. Next, joining R5(A, B, C, E) with R1(B, D) on B gives R(A, B, C, D, E). Since B -> D holds in R1, and B is an attribute in R5, the common attribute B is a key for R1(B, D). Therefore, the decomposition is Lossless.

Step 4: Dependency Preservation Check.
Original FDs:
- A -> BC: Preserved in R4(A, B, C).
- CD -> E: Attributes C, D, E are split across relations. F' = {B->D, E->A, A->BC}. Let's check if CD -> E can be inferred from F'.
(CD)^+ under F' unioned: C+ = C, D+ = D. CD -> E cannot be derived from projections. Thus, CD -> E is NOT preserved.
Conclusion: The decomposition is lossless but not dependency-preserving.

rubric.criterion: Derivation of attribute closures and identification of candidate keys ({A} and {E})
Identification of BCNF violations (e.g., B->D and E->A)
Step-by-step BCNF decomposition resulting in final relations (R1, R3, R4)
Rigorous proof and analysis of Lossless Join property
Rigorous proof and analysis of Dependency Preservation property

own_words_criteria: Finding all superkeys using attribute closure
Breaking relations recursively at non-superkey functional dependency violations
Verifying common attributes contain a key for lossless joins
Checking closure of projected functional dependencies

questions.question: Design a comprehensive recovery protocol using Strict Two-Phase Locking (Strict 2PL) and ARIES algorithm for a distributed flight reservation system during concurrent system crashes.
questions.justification: Requires designing an integrated concurrency control and recovery architecture combining Strict 2PL and ARIES for a distributed transactional system.
questions.model_answer:
Design Architecture for Distributed Flight Reservation System:

1. Concurrency Control via Strict Two-Phase Locking (Strict 2PL):
- All shared locks (S-locks) and exclusive locks (X-locks) acquired by transactions during seat reservation or ticket booking must be held until the transaction explicitly commits or aborts.
- Prevents cascading rollbacks and ensures serializability by eliminating dirty reads across concurrent booking agents.

2. Recovery Protocol using ARIES (Algorithms for Recovery and Isolation Exploiting Semantics):
- ARIES operates in three precise phases during system restart: Analysis, Redo, and Undo.
- Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) is maintained globally with Log Sequence Numbers (LSNs) stamped on every log record, dirty page table (DPT), and transaction table (TT).

Phase I: Analysis Phase
- Scans forward from the last known checkpoint log record.
- Reconstructs the Transaction Table and Dirty Page Table (DPT) as they existed at the moment of the crash.
- Identifies the smallest `recLSN` in the DPT to determine the starting point for the Redo phase.

Phase II: REDO Phase (Repeating History)
- Repeats all actions (committed, active, and aborted transactions) starting from the minimum `recLSN` found in the Analysis phase.
- For each log record found (update, commit, abort), re-applies the change and updates the page's pageLSN.
- Brings the database state to the exact point of the crash.

Phase III: UNDO Phase
- Reverses the operations of all transactions that were active (uncommitted) at the time of the crash.
- Processes active transactions in reverse chronological order using the transaction's undoNextLSN pointers.
- Writes Compensation Log Records (CLRs) for every undone operation to prevent infinite redo loops during subsequent crashes, ensuring crash recovery convergence in distributed flight inventory updates.

rubric.criterion: Design and rationale of Strict 2PL for concurrency and cascading rollback avoidance
Architecture of ARIES logging mechanisms (LSN, DPT, Transaction Table)
Detailed specification of the Analysis phase
Detailed specification of the Redo phase (Repeating History)
Detailed specification of the Undo phase and Compensation Log Records (CLRs)

own_words_criteria: Holding exclusive locks until commit or abort
Scanning forward from the last checkpoint in Analysis
Replaying history forward from the minimum recLSN
Rolling back active transactions and writing CLRs in Undo
